learning_objective: 🎯 Master the art of writing for the ear and the eye! Learn how radio scripts paint pictures with sound, and television scripts blend audio with compelling visuals.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Radio is a 'blind' medium. The scriptwriter must rely entirely on spoken words, music, and sound effects (SFX) to create a visual picture in the listener's mind. Sentences must be short, conversational, and instantly understandable.

Television is an audiovisual medium. A TV script balances what the audience sees (action, camera angles) with what they hear (dialogue, background music). If the visuals show the action, the dialogue shouldn't repeat it.
Radio scripts clearly label SFX and music cues, often written in capital letters. TV scripts often use a two-column format (Video on the left, Audio on the right) or standard screenplay formatting.
Dialogue in scripts must sound natural, like real people talking. It shouldn't be overly formal or literary. People use contractions (don't, can't) and interrupt each other in real life!

TV scripts use specific terminology to move between scenes, such as 'Fade In' (gradually appearing from black), 'Cut To' (an instant change to the next scene), and 'Dissolve' (one image fading into another).

fun_activity.title: 🔊 The Blindfold Challenge
fun_activity.instructions: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds in your home or on the street for 2 minutes. Write down 5 distinct sounds you heard. Now, write a 3-line radio script using ONLY those sound effects to tell a tiny story, without using any dialogue!

exam_tips: 📌 When writing a radio script for an exam, ALWAYS include sound effect cues (e.g., [SFX: Door creaks open, footsteps on wood]). This proves you understand the medium.
📌 For TV scripts, remember the golden rule: 'Show, Don't Tell'. Let the camera do the work instead of relying on the narrator.
📌 Radio language should be simple and direct. Avoid complex, flowery sentences that are hard for a news anchor to read aloud.
quick_recap: ⭐ Radio is the 'theater of the mind'—your words build the sets and costumes.
⭐ Television requires dual-channel thinking: visual action and audio dialogue working together.
⭐ Scripts are blueprints for production, not final products meant to be read like novels.
